As a first-term MP, it's been really heartening to see

are looking at really specific issues that affect people in New
Zealand. And

Zealand is. And it has been really heartening to
see committee members really

So I commend everyone here, and thank you for your time,
going through the submissions and really scrutinizing this bill
in particular so that we can make sure that it is fit for purpose
for the modern country that New Zealand is.
One of the best things about Aotearoa is our stories,
our stories told by our creatives
and our artists. Their work entertains
us, it educate us, and it prompts us to think about
ourselves and the world around us.
Artists invoke

Satire and comedy specifically are some of the best

ideas that facilitate vital
discussion and critical engagement, particularly in
a democratic society. However,
currently,
as the law stands, artists who use material for
purposes of comedy and satire are at risk of copyright
infringement. This can make for
costly legal fees or the threat of costly
legal fees, impedes expression, and can make our
artists afraid of creating meaningful work.
Over the last year, since this bill was pulled from the biscuit tin,
very excitedly,
I have talked to many artists from many fields about
whether they have ever been sued or had threat of sue.
And what's interesting is, not a lot of court cases have
actually been brought in New Zealand,

So people are in the middle of creating something, a company hears

And so, we've heard that story time and time and again, and
that's art that is
not being released to the world and is dampening the
expression that artists have.
The other intent of this bill are--
So the intent of the Copyright
Amendment Bill is to add provision to that Copyright Act
1994, like over 30 years old, to clarify that
work being used for the purpose of parody and satire does not infringe
copyright. So the other intent of this bill is to ensure New
Zealand copyright laws are equipped to deal with both the
changing media landscape, we can probably all agree that the
internet's changed a little bit over the last 30 years, and bring
our legislation into line with other countries such as Australia,
Canada, France, Spain, and Germany.
Our copyright laws should reflect the changing nature of our media landscape.
In the digital age, social media and the freedom of
information that happens on the internet means that our
copyright laws need to align with this
change. There's been a variety of artists and
creatives who have spoken in support of the bill,

legal challenges. Because currently, in New Zealand,
artists can be sued for things that artists across

see our creatives leading on the
world stage. But what they are doing internationally, they could be sued

because,

remove risk of financial pressures due to being fined for copyright,

disrespect of Māori works or taonga.
Ongoing engagement through this process with Māori and
iwi,

All right. Our next submitter is We Create Incorporated via Zoom.
Tēnā koutou katoa. Thank you for having me this afternoon.
Good afternoon, and welcome.
We Create is the alliance of 40 of Aotearoa's major
creative industry associations, representing over 30,000
creatives, support people, and creative businesses across every
creative discipline from screen to music, book publishing, media
design, performing arts, and digital production.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to our written submission.
I'd like to use this time to bring three things to your attention that I
think are essential context for your deliberations, and
also that I hope will stay with you as members of both this committee and of
Parliament beyond this bill.
Firstly, the bill arrives in the middle of a technology revolution, and this
changes everything in regard to what this bill can and should
do. When Parliament last made a substantive change to the
Copyright Act, ChatGPT didn't exist.
Neither did Sora, Midjourney, or the dozens of other generative AI
tools that are now trained on the creative work of New Zealanders, trained
without consent, without compensation, and without any usable legal
framework for redress.
In early June, Minister Brewer announced that Cabinet has invited him to report
back in March next year on a possible copyright framework for generative
AI in New Zealand. We welcome that, but it underlines something
important, that the government itself has now acknowledged that the relationship
between copyright and AI is unresolved.
This matters for the bill before you today.
A parody and satire exception that is not precisely written does not just affect
the question of whether someone can post a meme or make a satirical song
or make a joke. It affects the terms in which AI companies,
most of whom are operating at massive scale across borders and with enormous
commercial interests that don't benefit New Zealand, can claim that their use
of New Zealand creators' work is lawfully permitted.
We're not suggesting that this bill is an AI bill.
What we are saying is that the days of drafting copyright exceptions as if
only individual human users will rely on them are over.
Mm.
Every new exception in the Copyright Act is now a potential license for
automated large-scale commercial exploitation by some of
the world's most powerful companies.
We believe that the select committee should be alert to this.
Secondly, the bill as drafted is not fit for purpose.
Our written submission sets out WeCreate's position in detail, but I want to
highlight what our member organizations, these are organizations that work with
copyright in practice every day, have told us.
Their support for a narrowly drawn exception, a carefully
defined parody and satire exception modeled on what Australia introduced in
2006, is not something that the creative sector categorically
opposes. Exceptions should not be implemented in isolation,
however, which is what this bill would do.
They should be considered in line with an overall assessment of the act,
including changes that support the needs of our creators.
In particular, our members consistently flag that the legislative drafting must
do the work that enforcement cannot.
New Zealand is a low to no enforcement jurisdiction for
copyright. The cost of taking a copyright infringement case
to the High Court, and I've been there myself, is prohibitive for individual
creators and small creative businesses.
In this environment, an imprecise exception does not produce balanced
outcomes. It produces a free pass.
Introducing a vague exception in a non-enforcement jurisdiction
and leaving matters to a hypothetical but unlikely court case
is not productive or helpful. Further, the bill does not
define parody, and it doesn't define satire.
These are not minor drafting details.
They're essential load-bearing elements of the exception.
We know that Australian academics have criticized their equivalent position,
sorry, provision for this exact omission, and US courts have been
embroiled in constant disputes about the meaning of parody for decades.
New Zealand has the advantage of being able to learn from all of this, and we
should take it.
Critically, this bill is silent on mātauranga Māori, taonga works,
and traditional cultural expression.
These occupy a distinct moral and ethical space in Aotearoa,
New Zealand. The recommendation in relation to mātauranga Māori that are
contained in the Wai 262 report remain unimplemented,
and we should not be passing a Copyright Act amendment that compounds
existing inadequacies in the protection of taonga works by
creating a broad, undefined exception that could be used to
justify culturally harmful uses as protected commentary.
Thirdly, what this
committee does next matters more than this bill.
I want
to be direct with you about something.
This bill may or may not reach the House before the election.
Whether it does or doesn't, the copyright issues that have surfaced will not go
away. They will be on the agenda for the next parliament, the one after that, and
every parliament in the foreseeable future because the technology disruption
driving them is accelerating, not slowing.
The creative sector contributes $18.5 billion to our GDP.
That's 4.3% of the total. Creative exports have
grown at 9% compound annual growth since 2015, making
the sector the fifth largest export earner.
So this is not a small sector that's asking for special treatment.
This is a major economic contributor asking for a regulatory
framework that is fit for the digital economy.
The Copyright Act 1994 is 32 years old.
It predates streaming, predates social media, and it definitely
predates generative AI.
The sector acknowledges that the government has recently announced a copyright term
extension. We note that this is a free trade agreement obligation, and
legislation to implement the new term has yet to be drafted.
A further announcement has been made on a shortlist of other copyright reforms.
This includes my least favorite copyright term, locked up.
Can I ask that the next time you hear locked up used in relation to
copyright, you think about the artist who created the work-
Mm
... their connection to that work, and their moral and economic rights.
The list of further reforms has not been informed by recent engagement with
WeCreate or our members. It's not extensive and doesn't
prioritize the areas of copyright that we know need to be changed to
effectively protect New Zealand's artists and creative businesses.
We're asking this committee to use your report to call for a comprehensive,
creator-centered review of the act.
The review needs to be undertaken with appropriate resourcing in both MBIE and
the Ministry for Culture and Heritage in a reasonable timeline and with a
mandate to legislate. The creative professionals and creative businesses in
Aotearoa deserve copyright law that reflects the world they are actually
working in. A world where their work can be scraped, stolen,
synthesized
, distributed at scale, and where the law should be their first line
of protection, not an afterthought. Thank you.

Great. Thank you very much for your submission this afternoon. Appreciate it.
